A Claude Code session running in your laptop terminal inherits every constraint of that laptop. Opening two sessions in the same repository means sharing one working directory, where concurrent edits and local server ports collide. Every session runs with your full local user permissions, and closing the lid or losing Wi-Fi stops the work mid-turn. Cloud sessions remove all three constraints by moving each task into an isolated virtual machine. This post breaks down how cloud sessions are structured and which tasks belong in the cloud versus on your laptop.
At a Glance Every cloud session boots a fresh virtual machine (VM), clones your repository onto a new branch, and leaves its changes on that branch ready to open as a pull request. Cloud sessions are included at no extra machine charge on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans, drawing from your existing Claude Code usage allowance. Because sessions share neither files nor ports, they fit parallel bug fixes and verification loops that run a test suite dozens of times in a row. GitHub permissions cause most first-run failures: signing in with GitHub and installing the Claude GitHub App are two separate steps. About the Original Post Addy Osmani published this 18-minute field guide on October 6, 2026. Rather than staying abstract, the post runs four real cloud sessions against a small sample repository and shares the actual transcripts, diffs, and wall-clock timings. It is written for developers who already use Claude Code in a local terminal and want to know when to offload work to the cloud. Source: Claude Code in the cloud.
Three Tasks on Three Machines at Once The sample repository, tidepool, is a small Node API that predicts tides across three fictional harbors. It has three separate issues: a test that fails roughly one run in four, API documentation that has drifted from the implementation, and plain string-concatenated logs. The author launches three cloud sessions within 16 seconds, assigning one task to each.
Figure 1. Horizontal axis shows seconds elapsed since launching the first session. Hatched bars mark demo repository setup, where a standard GitHub clone normally happens; each dot represents one tool call. Source: Original post.
Each session ran for 61 to 72 seconds, and all three wrapped up within 87 seconds of the first launch:
Flaky test: Claude traced the failure to a race condition in TtlCache.get, where a second request for the same key arriving mid-fetch triggered a duplicate loader call. It cached the in-flight promise and ran npm test 40 times in a row with zero failures. API docs: Claude started the server, queried every endpoint with curl, and fixed five mismatches between the responses and the documentation. Structured logs: Claude replaced string logs with JSON output and added five tests. When one test failed during verification, Claude traced it to the same cache race condition VM 1 was fixing, left the out-of-scope cache code untouched, and noted the dirty test run in its summary. Because each session had its own repository clone, process space, and branch, the documentation and logging sessions could both boot the API server simultaneously without port conflicts. Isolation has a flip side: the logging session could not see the cache fix happening next door. When splitting parallel work, cut along clean file boundaries and expect adjacent sessions to flag pre-existing bugs that another session is already fixing.
Anatomy of a Cloud Session Inside each session, the VM sits inside a strict boundary while credentials and network controls stay outside it.
Figure 2. Left (START OR CHECK FROM) shows where sessions can be launched—and monitored from browser, mobile, or desktop. Center (FRESH VM PER SESSION) shows the isolated VM, while right (OUTSIDE THE VM) shows the proxies handling credentials and network policy. Source: Original post.
Four architectural choices shape day-to-day usage:
Component How cloud sessions handle it Machine A fresh VM per task; sessions never share files, processes, or ports GitHub token Never enters the VM; a proxy issues a short-lived credential scoped to push only to that session’s working branch Configuration Repository CLAUDE.md, rules, and skills travel with the clone, while your personal ~/.claude stays on your laptop Idle VMs Reclaimed after inactivity; reopening restores the conversation in a new VM, so uncommitted file edits do not survive Cloud sessions do not replace local sessions. Tasks that depend on local-only resources—a local database with test data, internal services behind a VPN, a GPU, or a mobile simulator—still belong on your laptop, as does rapid UI iteration where you check a local browser every few seconds. Organizations under Zero Data Retention policies also stay local-only because cloud sessions are disabled there.
Workloads That Fit the Cloud From the seven workflows in the original guide, four stand out for everyday engineering work:
Firing off parallel small fixes: Run claude --cloud "task description" once per task. Because cloud sessions clone the current branch from GitHub remote, push your local commits first. Write each prompt with three specifics: what is broken, what done looks like, and which command proves it. Demanding proof of a fix: Because the cloud VM burns remote compute rather than your laptop CPU, you can ask for thorough verification—such as running the full test suite 40 times in a single loop to confirm a race condition is gone. Figure 3. The runs=40 fails=0 output at the bottom confirms 40 consecutive clean runs, followed by Claude’s root-cause writeup. Source: Original post.
Foreground bash commands time out after 2 minutes by default (up to 10 minutes max) and can continue running in the background for up to 30 minutes. You can raise those defaults via BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS and BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS.
Planning locally, executing in the cloud: For larger changes, align on an implementation plan interactively on your laptop first, hand execution off to a cloud VM, and pull the finished branch back down when needed. flowchart LR A["Local plan mode<br/>Align on plan"] -->|"Commit and push"| B["claude --cloud<br/>Execute plan"] B -->|"Push branch"| C["claude --teleport<br/>Pull into terminal"] C --> D["Finish by hand"] Running claude --teleport brings both the cloud session’s Git branch and its conversation history into your local terminal. The branch must already be pushed, and your local working tree should be clean—if uncommitted changes exist, Claude Code offers to stash them.
Running untrusted code: Testing an external contributor’s PR or a new dependency’s install script on your laptop exposes local SSH keys and cloud CLI logins sitting in the same user account. A disposable cloud VM holds none of those secrets and lets you restrict outbound network access down to None. Keep two caveats in mind: even with network set to None, requests to the Anthropic API still leave the VM, and the session can still push to its own branch. The guide also covers starting or checking sessions from the mobile app, using Auto-fix to resolve CI failures and review comments on PRs, and scheduling recurring routines from cron schedules or GitHub events.
GitHub Permissions and Environment Setup GitHub access relies on two separate layers. Signing in with GitHub only verifies your identity; repository visibility for private repos comes from installing the Claude GitHub App on the user account or organization that owns the repository. When a private repo is missing from the picker, walk through this check:
flowchart TD A["Private repo missing<br/>from the picker"] --> D{"Claude GitHub App installed<br/>on owning account or org?"} D -->|"No"| E["Install App on that account or org<br/>Org installs need owner approval"] D -->|"Yes"| F["Check App repo selection scope<br/>and SAML SSO authorization"] Public repositories work with GitHub sign-in alone. In the browser flow, private organization repositories appear only after the App is installed on that organization. If you already use the gh CLI locally, running /web-setup inside Claude Code can pass your gh token instead, granting access to whatever repositories that token can reach without the GitHub App—though Team and Enterprise plans require an owner to enable Quick setup first. Auto-fix, GitHub-event routines, and projects always require the GitHub App regardless of setup path.
Once GitHub is connected, the VM needs a working test environment so the session can verify its own changes. The Default image already covers most JavaScript, Python, Go, and Rust repositories. System packages belong in a setup script, which runs as root, must exit 0, and gets cached only if it finishes within 5 minutes. Project dependency steps like npm install fit better in a SessionStart hook inside .claude/settings.json, where both local and cloud sessions execute them identically. Commands for running integration suites belong in CLAUDE.md, since your personal ~/.claude directory never enters the cloud VM.
Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation, not part of the original post.
Watching the logging session hit the out-of-scope cache bug, leave src/cache.js alone, and document the failure in its summary is a great model for parallel agent work. Whether you are splitting backend services or data pipelines across concurrent sessions, stating explicit file boundaries in each prompt—and instructing the agent to report rather than fix out-of-scope failures—prevents painful merge conflicts later.
Whether a cloud session returns a PR you can merge quickly depends heavily on the verification command in your prompt. For data engineering tasks, asking an agent to “run a validation query comparing row counts and totals against the baseline table” beats “fix the SQL query” for the exact same reason a 40-run test loop beats a single pass: the session brings back numeric proof alongside the diff.
Leaving ~/.claude behind on your laptop creates healthy pressure for engineering teams. Because cloud sessions only know how to build, test, and lint your project if those instructions live in the repository (CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, shared skills, and MCP configs), onboarding a cloud VM ends up documenting the repo for new human teammates at the same time.
What to Try First Open claude.ai/code, connect GitHub, and verify that the Claude GitHub App is installed on the account or organization owning your main private repositories. Pick two small backlog items that touch separate files, push your current branch, and launch both in parallel via claude --cloud—including an explicit verification command in each prompt. Check whether your repository’s CLAUDE.md states the exact command to run tests; if not, add a one-line instruction today. Original post: Claude Code in the cloud: a field guide to cloud sessions
summary: How Claude Code cloud sessions isolate each task in its own virtual machine and Git branch, which workloads belong in the cloud versus on your laptop, and how to avoid common GitHub setup pitfalls.

Long sessions in Claude Code make it easy to lose track of how much conversation context has accumulated, or what a file-deletion command is about to wipe out before it runs. Mods let you attach small custom programs to Claude Code to surface that state or step in before an action executes. Using a weather-style context indicator as the main example, this post walks through how mods run, how to build one, and what to watch out for when sharing them.
At a Glance A mod is a small JavaScript or TypeScript file that runs alongside your Claude Code session. It can inspect session state, modify an action right before execution, or render custom status information in the terminal UI. You can ask Claude in plain language to generate a mod for you, or write one yourself starting from an empty plugin folder. Mods live inside plugins, which package extensions for installation, and connect to session activity through hooks that fire when specific events occur. The post walks through three examples: Token Weather for live context usage, Blast Radius for previewing destructive commands, and Replay Theater for stepping through file edits. About the Original Post Addy Osmani published this tutorial on October 1, 2026. Following the examples requires Claude Code 2.1.287 or later. Because you can start by describing what you want in plain English without memorizing the API upfront, the guide fits regular Claude Code users who want to adapt the terminal workflow to their own habits. Source: Getting started with Claude Code mods.
How Mods Work Under the Hood Whenever Claude Code calls a tool or finishes a response, it emits an event. An event signals that an action is happening, and a hook is the custom handler function you attach to run at that moment—for instance, logging changed files right after an edit completes.
Mod files sit inside a plugin directory, where hooks.json points to the code module to load. Inside that module’s register function, on(event, hook) binds specific events to your handler code.
Multiple hooks run in sequence like middleware. Calling next(e) hands the event to the next handler in the chain; once the chain finishes, Claude Code performs the underlying action. That structure gives each hook three distinct ways to act:
Observe: Let the original action run and record the outcome, such as tracking which files were edited during a turn. Rewrite: Modify the event payload before passing it forward, such as swapping a command for a safer variant. Respond: Return a result directly without calling next, stopping a tool call before it reaches execution. Everything hinges on whether your handler calls next. Calling next lets the event pass through any remaining hooks to the original action and returns the result back up the chain. Returning early without next ends the action inside your hook.
Beyond tool calls, events cover prompt submission, turn start and end, custom slash commands, and ui.render for drawing terminal UI elements.
Modules execute inside a restricted sandbox rather than a browser DOM or a full Node runtime. Instead of standard system APIs, your code interacts with the session and terminal screen through the $ object provided by Claude Code.
Traditional configuration hooks spawn a fresh shell command each time they fire, whereas a mod stays alive for the entire session. Because it persists in memory, a mod can retain state across turns, update status lines, open interactive panels, and register new slash commands or model-callable tools.
First Example: Token Weather The context window is the total span of conversation history and file content the model can hold at once. At the end of each turn, Token Weather reads how full that window is and renders a single status line above the prompt, pairing token counts with a weather label that shifts as usage climbs.
Context usage Label What it signals Under 25% Clear Plenty of headroom left 25–49% Cloudy Context is steadily filling up 50–74% Showers More than half the window is used 75–89% Storm Running low on remaining context 90% and above Compact soon Time to consider compacting the conversation Alongside total tokens used, the bar shows a 12-turn sparkline of recent history and the token delta from the latest turn, making both current capacity and recent growth rate visible at a glance.
The session screenshots from the original post show a 200k context window crossing 18%, 67%, and 81%.
Figure 1. The single-line Token Weather indicator from the original post. Labels progress from Clear through Showers to Storm as the 200k window fills, while the mini bars on the right track per-turn growth. Source: Original post.
Each threshold crossing updates both the weather label and its color: 18% sits in Clear, 67% in Showers, and 81% in Storm.
The fastest way to build it is to launch claude and describe the indicator you want. With hot reload enabled—so Claude Code re-reads modified plugin files without a restart—the new status bar appears as soon as the turn finishes. Follow-up tweaks like lowering the Storm threshold to 70% can also be requested in plain English.
Writing the mod by hand takes roughly 80 lines of code:
Launch claude --plugin-dir to load the plugin under development, reloading automatically whenever you save a file. Read current window consumption via $.session.usage() and store per-turn history in $.state. Plain module-level variables reset on hot reload, whereas $.state survives reloads for the life of the session. Check plugin structure with claude plugin validate and verify behavior with claude plugin test. Saving edits to tweak the UI reloads the module cleanly while keeping the turn history accumulated in $.state.
Sharing Mods and Two Larger Examples To distribute a mod, you publish a marketplace manifest in a GitHub repository listing the available plugins. Other users register that repository with /plugin marketplace add, install the mod via /plugin install, and pick up changes with /reload-plugins.
A mod runs on your machine with the same OS permissions as Claude Code itself, and community-published mods are not official Anthropic code. The module sandbox limits which JavaScript APIs a mod can call directly, not whether installed code is safe to trust. Treat third-party mods like any software package: read the repository first and install only from authors you trust.
The post closes with two larger examples built on the same hook model:
Blast Radius: Intercepts destructive commands such as rm -rf, git reset --hard (which discards uncommitted work), and force-pushes before they run, computes their impact, and opens a confirmation panel with Proceed and Cancel options. In the original example, rm -rf build previews 9 files (1.1 MB) slated for deletion. Because the mod parses only the raw command string, it can miss command substitutions like $(…), shell aliases, or scripts that invoke rm internally. The author frames it as a helpful guardrail rather than a hard security boundary—use permission rules when you need guaranteed blocking. Replay Theater: Observes Edit and Write tool calls during a turn without altering file writes, then lets you press r or run /replay to step through before-and-after diffs one change at a time. Figure 2. Blast Radius lists two uncommitted files that git reset --hard would wipe out, pausing execution until the user picks Proceed or Cancel. Source: Original post.
Figure 3. Replay Theater walks through file edits one step at a time with Prev, Next, and Close controls. Source: Original post.
Non-destructive commands pass straight through without interruption; only flagged patterns pause for human confirmation.
Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation and hands-on testing, not part of the original post.
Designing a mod gets much simpler once you decide upfront whether it observes, rewrites, or responds early. File-edit history belongs in a passive observer, whereas destructive commands warrant pausing execution to preview impact. The Blast Radius pattern translates directly to database tooling as well: before an agent runs a query, a hook can preview affected tables or row counts and wait for explicit approval.
Keeping context fill level and recent per-turn growth visible removes the guesswork around when to compact a session. Pairing cumulative totals with recent deltas works well for other operational agent metrics too, such as tool-call latency or retry counts.
Because installed mods inherit Claude Code’s local permissions, a flawed or malicious community mod can affect your workspace directly. Teams sharing internal mods should review authorship, file access, and shell execution paths before installation, just as they would for internal CLI packages.
Rebuilding all three examples directly in Claude Code 2.1.289 surfaced a few practical constraints worth knowing before combining multiple mods:
Only one mod can own the single status line above the prompt at a time. When Token Weather occupies that slot, Replay Theater cannot place its r shortcut prompt in the same spot, so we exposed edit counts in the status bar and opened the viewer via /replay instead. Because Blast Radius inspects only the literal command string, paths containing ~ or $HOME are not expanded and appear only as "not expanded". Remote commit counts for force-push warnings also reflect the last local git fetch rather than live remote state. A single risky command can trigger both the mod’s confirmation panel and Claude Code’s built-in permission prompt back to back. In non-interactive runs such as claude -p, where nobody can answer a prompt, risky commands are always rejected. Running several mods together means sharing scarce UI slots and coordinating pre-execution hooks with built-in permission rules. Check where each mod renders and where it intercepts the hook chain before stacking them in one workspace.
What to Try First Run claude --version in your terminal and confirm you are on 2.1.287 or later before testing the mod APIs from this guide. Pick one metric you want visible throughout a session—for example, ask Claude to build a one-line mod showing current context percentage and the token jump from the previous turn—and watch how it behaves across a real task. Read every file in a mod repository before installing or sharing it with teammates, checking which files it reads or writes and whether it intercepts or executes commands. Original post: Getting started with Claude Code mods
summary: How Claude Code mods work as small in-session JavaScript or TypeScript modules, walked through with the Token Weather context gauge, Blast Radius command checks, Replay Theater diff viewer, and plugin sharing.

You edit a prompt, run two or three sample inputs, and the answers look sharper. How do you know whether the change improved overall behavior or only fixed the exact examples on your screen? Relying on gut feel after a few spot checks makes regressions easy to miss. This post explains how to build representative evaluation sets and verify iterative changes against held-out test cases.
At a Glance An evaluation set pairs realistic task inputs with grading rules; a useful eval separates stronger configurations from weaker ones and produces stable scores across repeat runs. Inside Claude Code’s claude-api skill, /claude-api build-eval interviews you to assemble an eval inside your project, and /claude-api hillclimb tests one targeted edit at a time. Splitting examples into a train set (used to inspect failures) and a held-out test set catches overfitting, where edits memorize the examples you read without helping unseen requests. About the Original Post Lance Martin published this playbook on the claude.devblog on September 28, 2026. It is written for developers maintaining LLM applications or skills who want a structured way to measure whether prompt, tool, or model changes actually move the needle.
What Makes a Good Eval, and How build-eval Works An eval tests how well an application or skill handles a defined job. For a customer support agent, for example, real incoming tickets serve as the test cases (the eval set), and code or a judge model scores whether the agent made the right routing or refund decision (the grader). The original post highlights four properties of a reliable eval:
Representative of real work. Cherry-picking inputs that are easy to write or easy to grade distorts the mix of requests your system actually sees in production. Able to separate capability tiers. Stronger models or higher effort budgets should generally score higher. Flat scores across tiers usually point to vague task prompts or flawed grading criteria. Headroom to improve. Even the strongest setup should score well below 100% so future gains remain visible. That gap is the eval’s headroom, though items that every run fails should be checked for impossible or contradictory instructions. Repeatable across runs. Drifting effort settings or leftover files and Git history leaking answers from earlier runs invalidate score comparisons. Clean, identical run conditions are what let you attribute score deltas to your edit. Building an eval solely out of cases the current model gets wrong skews the benchmark toward one model’s blind spots. Instead, the author recommends collecting cases where a domain human can articulate why the problem is hard, supplemented by real failures from production logs, bug reports, and support tickets.
Running /claude-api build-eval launches an interactive interview that builds an eval inside your repository. It gathers test cases in priority order: production logs first, then bug reports and tickets, 5–10 hand-written examples, and finally synthetic cases derived from your codebase. Claude surfaces every candidate case for your review before locking the set in.
For grading, build-eval starts with the cheapest reliable check. Exact numbers or structured outputs get deterministic code assertions, while open-ended text responses use an LLM judge against explicit criteria. It then runs sample grades and shows them to you so you can spot cases where the grader disagrees with your own judgment.
Next, it records a baseline score before any edits begin, checking whether repeat grading produces consistent verdicts and whether timeouts or output-length caps truncated any responses. Catching execution-environment glitches early keeps you from mistaking harness bugs for model failures.
Human review happens at two explicit checkpoints: right after assembling candidate inputs, and right after inspecting sample grader outputs.
Hillclimbing: One Change at a Time Against a Held-Out Split Hillclimbing means making one small adjustment, re-running the benchmark, keeping the edit if scores improve, and repeating. Changing five things at once hides which edit helped and which hurt, so each round isolates a single hypothesis.
The main trap is overfitting. Hardcoding rules tailored to the exact wording of known eval questions lifts benchmark numbers while failing on fresh phrasing. Overfitting can creep into any part of the harness: prompts, tool definitions, or the orchestration code wrapped around the model.
To guard against that, /claude-api hillclimb randomly partitions your eval into train and test splits. “Train” here does not mean updating model weights; it simply marks the subset of failures Claude is allowed to read when diagnosing errors and proposing prompt or harness edits. The held-out test split stays unseen during diagnosis and checks whether each edit generalizes to unfamiliar cases.
Each round reads failure logs from the train split, proposes a single patch, applies it, and re-scores both splits. A patch stays only when both train and test scores improve; if only the train score climbs or either score drops, the loop reverts the change.
When scores flatten for two or three rounds, the tool categorizes the remaining failures to check whether ambiguous test prompts or harness bugs are capping performance. Once the run finishes, it leaves your repository at the highest-scoring test checkpoint. If the net gain falls inside run-to-run noise, it flags that no real improvement was confirmed and advises against merging.
Figure 1. From left: editable target, fixed model and execution harness, train and test evaluation splits, and the keep-or-revert gate. The analyzer reads failures from the train split only. A patch stays only when both scores improve; if only the train score rises or either score drops, the loop reverts it. Source: Original post.
Whenever train accuracy rises while test accuracy stalls, the loop treats the patch as overfit and rolls it back. Sustained plateaus pause patch generation altogether to weed out broken eval items before starting another round.
Two Case Studies In the customer support benchmark, 44 tickets were split into 30 train tickets and 14 held-out test tickets, measuring how often the system reached the right handling decision. Across the 30 train tickets, iterative changes moved accuracy and cost through four steps:
Configuration and change Decision accuracy Cost per ticket Baseline: Opus 4.8 default (high) effort 74.4% 4.6¢ Cleaned-up prompt on Opus 5.5 low effort 87.8% 1.9¢ Sonnet 5 low effort 88.9% 1¢ Refined prompt linking routing rules to refund limits 98.9% 1¢ Evaluating the final setup on the 14 held-out test tickets confirmed the gain: test accuracy reached 90.5% compared to 78.6% at baseline, while per-ticket cost dropped to roughly one-fifth of the starting point. Checking the held-out split is what shows the prompt fixes generalized beyond the 30 tickets inspected during tuning.
Figure 2. Horizontal axis shows cost per ticket (log scale) and vertical axis shows decision accuracy on the train split. Moving up and to the left means higher accuracy at lower cost. Source: Original post.
Steps 1 through 4 trace the optimization path across model tiers and prompt edits. Moving from step 2 to step 3 held accuracy nearly flat while halving cost, and step 4 jumped accuracy via a targeted prompt clarification. Because Figure 2 plots the 30-ticket train split, always read it alongside the 14-ticket test split above.
The second case study evaluated the claude-api skill itself, a bundle of reference instructions Claude loads for API tasks, climbing from 66% to roughly 88%. Filling eight missing feature sections lifted the score to 74%, and fixing an inaccurate type-definition table pushed it to 77%.
When progress stalled, failure classification revealed the model was generating deprecated API patterns. Adding a migration mapping table from old syntax to current syntax brought the score to 80%. From there, repairing flawed eval prompts and grading logic alongside further skill edits took the final number to around 88%. Because that last jump includes fixes to the test questions and grader themselves, do not read the entire jump from 80% to 88% as pure skill improvement.
Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation, not part of the original post.
When benchmark scores stop climbing, audit your eval questions and grader before churning through more prompt or model tweaks. Vague prompts or brittle grading logic penalize valid answers, just as the claude-api skill case uncovered. Keep score increases caused by fixing a broken grader separate from genuine quality gains in your system.
Evals are just as useful for cutting cost as for chasing higher accuracy. Once your baseline meets quality targets, the same eval set tells you quickly whether a smaller model or lower effort tier holds accuracy steady at a fraction of the spend.
Even on a small dataset, separate the examples you read while editing prompts from the examples you use to judge the edit. In the support benchmark, held-out test accuracy (90.5%) landed well below train accuracy (98.9%), a gap you would never see without a split. Small held-out sets still warrant follow-up checks on broader production traffic.
Verify that your yardstick works before swapping models or rewriting prompts; otherwise you cannot tell why a score moved.
What to Try First Pick one prompt running in production, pull a sample of real inputs from request logs, and write down what counts as a passing output for each case. Run your grader on a handful of responses and read the input, model answer, and grader verdict side by side to catch false passes or false failures early. Split those cases into two buckets: read failure details only from the train bucket when revising your prompt, and log both train and held-out test scores before and after each edit. Original post: Automating eval design and hillclimbing with Claude
summary: How the build-eval and hillclimb commands in Claude Code’s claude-api skill automate evaluation design and iterative prompt tuning without overfitting, illustrated with two benchmark case studies.

content:
Picking a model in the Claude app is a dropdown swap, whereas changing the model your application calls over the API touches request parameters and response parsing too. Moving to Sonnet 5.5 means checking more than the model ID string. This post breaks down when Sonnet 5.5 makes sense over Opus 5.5 and which API settings need updating when migrating from Sonnet 5.
At a Glance Sonnet 5.5 is the second model in the Claude 5.5 family after Opus 5.5, running 30% faster than Sonnet 5 and lowering task cost by up to 30% across most workloads. Per-token list prices match Sonnet 5; the savings come from using fewer tokens to finish the same job. Treat Sonnet 5.5 as the default for well-scoped everyday tasks, and reach for Opus 5.5 when work requires long multi-step judgment. Migrating API calls from Sonnet 5 requires checking thinking and tool_choice settings, along with computer use and advisor parameters if your integration uses them. About the Original Post Addy Osmani published this Playbooks guide on claude.dev on September 28, 2026. Written as a hands-on migration reference for developers integrating Claude through the API, it fits engineering teams weighing model selection, latency, and cost across coding tools or production agents.
Choosing Between Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 The original post draws the line around two questions: is the specification clear, and can you verify the output? Tasks that meet both criteria belong on Sonnet 5.5, including bug fixes, scoped feature work, docs, slide decks, spreadsheets, research, and code or content reviews.
Open-ended knowledge work and multi-step agentic coding, where the model reads files, edits code, runs tests, and sustains judgment across a long loop, belong on Opus 5.5 instead. At the time of publication, Anthropic also noted that Haiku 5.5 would arrive within a few weeks for high-volume workloads.
Figure 1. From left: original photo, followed by scenes rendered by Sonnet 5, Sonnet 5.5, and Opus 5.5. Rather than calling an image generator, each model wrote Python code to paint the image. Demo by Lance Martin; meant as a visual illustration rather than a formal benchmark. Source: Original post.
The demo drew inspiration from code-painting experiments by @jkeatn, using an original photograph by @IceSolst.
Look at how clearly the requirements and acceptance checks are defined rather than routing by task label alone.
Per million tokens, Sonnet 5.5 lists at $2 for input and $10 for output, while Opus 5.5 lists at $4 for input and $20 for output. Cache reads, which reuse a shared prompt prefix already sent in an earlier turn, cost $0.20 per million tokens on both models.
Price per 1M tokens Sonnet 5.5 Opus 5.5 Input $2 $4 Output $10 $20 Cache write · 5m $2.50 $5 Cache write · 1h $4 $8 Cache read $0.20 $0.20 Fresh input, output, and initial cache writes all cost twice as much on Opus 5.5 as on Sonnet 5.5; only cache reads match. Including batch processing and prompt caching, Sonnet 5.5 carries the exact same rate card as Sonnet 5.
Because the rate card did not budge between Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 5.5, comparing price tables tells you nothing about your actual bill. Lower task spend comes from finishing the same work in fewer tokens, which you can only measure by running representative tasks from your own workload.
Images consume input tokens as well. Sonnet 5.5 processes high-resolution images up to 2,576 pixels on the long edge, so a 2000×1500 image uses roughly 2.5× as many tokens as it did on Sonnet 4.6. Downscale images before sending them unless the task depends on reading fine print or dense UI details.
Sonnet 5.5 supports a 1M-token context window and up to 128k output tokens per response (M = million, k = thousand), with no beta header needed to unlock long context. Pass claude-sonnet-5-5 as the model ID in API requests.
Default effort, which controls how much compute the model spends reasoning, differs by environment: the Claude API defaults to high, while Claude Code defaults to medium.
API Breaking Changes When Migrating from Sonnet 5 This section covers code-level changes in API integrations. An HTTP 400 error means the API rejected the request format or parameter combination upfront, before the model ever ran.
First, thinking behavior changed. Sonnet 5.5 runs with thinking enabled by default, and sending thinking: {"type": "disabled"} now triggers a 400 error.
If you want to skip initial upfront reasoning and let the model think only between tool calls, set between_tools. That mode works only when effort is low, medium, or high; pairing between_tools with xhigh or max returns a 400 error. At xhigh or max, use adaptive thinking instead so the model scales its own reasoning depth.
Response parsing needs a check too. API responses return an array of typed content blocks such as thinking and text. Because the first element can now be a thinking block, client code that reads content[0].text blindly should be updated to inspect block types and extract text blocks explicitly.
Several feature-specific parameters also tightened:
Tool calling: Forcing tool execution by setting tool_choice to any or tool now returns a 400 error. The guide recommends sending auto and enabling strict: true so tool arguments conform to your schema. Computer use: On the Claude API and Google Cloud, screen interaction requires computer_toolset_20260801; declaring the older computer_20251124 tool returns a 400 error. Amazon Bedrock still accepted the older identifier when the post went live. Advisor tool: When Sonnet 5.5 runs as the executor asking another model for guidance, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, and Sonnet 5 are not supported as advisors. Valid advisor models include Opus 5.5, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5.5 itself. Progress updates: Notes longer than a sentence or two between tool calls arrive as progress-update thinking blocks, which come back empty under the default display configuration. Set thinking.display under adaptive thinking if your UI surfaces those status notes (between_tools returns plain text without extra setup). Because requests still succeed with HTTP 200 when notes are blank, verify this behavior explicitly in your UI. Inside Claude Code, running /claude-api migrate this project to claude-sonnet-5-5 scans your project to update the model ID and incompatible request parameters automatically.
Post-Migration Tuning Named effort tiers were recalibrated for Sonnet 5.5. Because thinking token volume at a given tier differs from Sonnet 5, do not assume your old effort setting will produce identical latency or spend.
For agentic coding with clear specs, the guide suggests starting at medium and moving to high only on longer or harder tasks. Save xhigh and max for workloads where evaluations confirm a quality lift; if extended reasoning pushes latency and cost too high at those tiers, test Opus 5.5 head-to-head instead.
Audit legacy prompt instructions written to patch older models. Refusal workarounds from Sonnet 5, manual tool-retry instructions, and anti-laziness nudges (“do not be lazy, write the full implementation”) should be stripped out and re-tested against your evals to see whether Sonnet 5.5 still needs them.
Minimum cacheable prefix length dropped from 1,024 tokens on Sonnet 5 to 512 tokens on Sonnet 5.5, though changing top-level effort between requests invalidates the cached prefix. Starting in Claude Code v2.1.284 on the Claude API, the sonnet alias resolves to Sonnet 5.5, while the default session model stays Opus 5.5.
Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation, not part of the original post.
Identical per-token rates can still produce noticeably different per-task bills. Because Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 5.5 share the exact same price table, the only way to judge migration savings is running a handful of recurring tasks on both models and comparing output quality alongside total tokens consumed.
Upgrading a model touches the whole harness (prompts, tool definitions, request config, and response parser), not just a model name constant. Keeping model parameters in one place and parsing response blocks by type rather than array index prevents brittle breakages on future upgrades.
Multi-step data agents can split work across models based on how verifiable each step is. Steps where a tool checks the output right away, such as generating and executing SQL against known schemas, fit Sonnet 5.5 well. Steps that interpret ambiguous results and decide follow-up investigation fit Opus 5.5, and both setups should be compared side by side on real queries.
What to Try First Search your codebase for thinking: {"type": "disabled"}, forced tool_choice values (any or tool), and hardcoded content[0].text reads, then update each call site against the migration rules above. Run a small batch of everyday tasks with identical inputs on Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 5.5, logging pass rates, input/output token counts, and wall-clock time side by side. Strip older compensating prompt rules on a test branch and run your evaluation cases to see which instructions are now dead weight. Original post: Building with Claude Sonnet 5.5
summary: When to pick Claude Sonnet 5.5 over Opus 5.5, why task costs drop even though per-token rates match Sonnet 5, and which API parameters now return 400 errors when migrating.
title: Before Switching to Sonnet 5.5: Opus Tradeoffs and API Settings That Break

content:
A rate card alone will not tell you what it costs to ship a feature in Claude Code. Every time the agent reads files, edits code, runs tests, and inspects failures, input and output tokens compound across the session. Using the pricing breakdown from Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 guide, this post explains how retry turns and prompt cache reuse shape your actual bill.
At a Glance On API list prices, Opus 5.5 cuts input and output token rates by 20% and cache-read rates by 60% compared to Opus 5. Holding token counts constant, the original post’s example session drops from $3.50 to $2.40, a reduction of roughly 31%. Four variables drive per-task cost: how many turns the loop runs, what share of input hits the prompt cache, how many output and reasoning tokens the model generates, and which model you pick. The most reliable benchmark is running one of your own tasks on both models and comparing the numbers in /usage. About the Original Post Addy Osmani published this guide on the claude.dev blog on September 25, 2026. It targets developers running Claude Code with an API key or managing usage across an engineering team. Because every dollar figure in the article comes from list prices applied to worked examples, the author recommends plugging in your own session numbers to verify the math on your workload.
What Drives the Cost of a Single Task Tokens measure the text a model reads and writes. Your prompt, file contents, and tool outputs count as input tokens, while the model’s replies and internal reasoning count as output tokens.
Claude Code works in a loop: it reads the conversation, calls a tool, inspects the tool result, and decides the next step. Fixing a bug might mean reading a file, applying a patch, running a test suite, and patching again when a test fails. Each pass through that cycle is one turn, and every turn resends the entire conversation accumulated so far, so input size grows as the session continues.
Resending the conversation does not mean paying fresh-input prices every time. When the beginning of a request matches an earlier turn, prompt caching serves that shared prefix at a discounted cache-read rate. Your cache hit rate is the share of total input tokens read from cache rather than billed as new input. In the breakdown below, K stands for thousand tokens and M stands for million tokens:
Turn count: Suppose a task’s active context grows from 20K to 120K tokens over 40 turns, totaling roughly 2.8M input tokens. With a 90% cache hit rate, input costs about $1.62. Finishing the same job in 25 turns brings input cost down to about $1.02 because the long conversation history is resent fewer times. Cache reads: Those same 2.8M input tokens would cost $11.20 with no cache at all, versus roughly $0.99 at a 96% cache hit rate. Most of the savings in long sessions come from reading repeated context at cached prices. Output tokens: On Opus 5.5, each output token costs 100 times as much as a cached input token. Generating 60K output tokens ($1.20) costs the same as reading 6M tokens from cache. Internal reasoning (thinking) is billed as output too, so raising effort pushes this number up. Model choice: Input, output, and cache unit rates all shift depending on which model runs the turn. All worked examples in the original post use Opus 5.5 API list prices per million tokens: $4 for fresh input, $20 for output, and $0.20 for cache reads. The simplified session totals omit the initial cache-write fee, which you still need to include when reconciling a full API invoice.
One practical way to cut wasted turns is giving Claude Code a test or build command upfront. Concrete failure output lets the model fix the exact problem instead of guessing across extra turns.
What Changed in Opus 5.5 The first shift is unit pricing. Cache reads dropped from one-tenth of the fresh-input price on Opus 5 to one-twentieth on Opus 5.5. On Pro, Max, and Team subscriptions, the original post notes that the same plan allowance covers roughly 25% more work than on Opus 5, alongside a higher 5-hour rolling cap. Keep subscription usage allowances separate from API dollar billing when reading these numbers.
For API-key users running long agent sessions, cheaper cache reads do most of the heavy lifting because repeated context dominates total token volume. Applying both models’ rate cards to the same example session cuts cache-read spend from $1.00 to $0.40.
Figure 1. API list prices per million tokens across input, output, and cache reads. Input and output dropped 20%, while cache reads dropped 60%. Source: Original post.
Example session item Opus 5 Opus 5.5 Cache read $1.00 $0.40 New input $1.00 $0.80 Output $1.50 $1.20 Total $3.50 $2.40 The Opus 5.5 column multiplies the example session’s token volumes by the new unit rates alongside the $0.40 cache-read figure from the original post:
New input: 200K × $4/M = $0.80 Output: 60K × $20/M = $1.20 Total: $0.40 + $0.80 + $1.20 = $2.40 The overall drop is ($3.50 − $2.40) ÷ $3.50 ≈ 31%. Because token counts stay fixed in this table, the comparison isolates the rate-card cut alone and excludes any savings from finishing in fewer turns. Cache reads show the steepest percentage drop, while output tokens remain the single largest cost item.
The second shift is how much work the model does per task. You may hear that Opus 5.5 is “40% cheaper,” which is Anthropic’s estimate for typical tasks at default settings rather than a 40% cut in token prices. That figure assumes Opus 5.5 finishes jobs using fewer tokens overall. Tightly scoped tasks take a similar number of turns on both models and save mainly the list-price difference, whereas open-ended tasks with broad codebase exploration and trial-and-error tend to widen the gap.
Practical Controls During a Session Check Verification Loops Before Raising Effort The effort setting tells the model how much compute to spend on reasoning across four standard tiers (low, medium, high, and xhigh) plus single-session max. Opus 5.5 defaults to medium, whereas Opus 5 defaulted to high. Because Opus 5.5 reasons more thoroughly at the same named tier, avoid carrying Opus 5 effort settings over unchanged.
Spending more on effort can still lower total session cost when extra reasoning prevents a retry spiral. In the original post’s math, adding 20K thinking tokens at high costs $0.40. Compare that with a 10-turn retry loop rereading 100K cached tokens per turn and producing 10K output tokens in total: 1M × $0.20/M + 10K × $20/M = $0.40. Preventing a retry loop of that size pays back the extra reasoning budget right away.
Follow a clear escalation order when a task stalls: first make sure the agent can run tests or a build to verify its own edits, then step up effort, and switch models last.
When to Switch Models The author uses Opus 5.5 for interactive sessions where a developer is watching the terminal, and reserves Fable 5.1 for long unattended runs or unfamiliar, thorny problems. Fable 5.1 lists at $10 input, $50 output, and $0.25 cache read per million tokens. Subagents that split off search or log-reading chores run on Sonnet or Haiku instead. A practical rule from the post: if Opus 5.5 gets stuck twice on the same problem at xhigh, hand that step to Fable 5.1 and drop back to Opus 5.5 once resolved.
Raising effort costs less than jumping up a model tier, so stop escalating as soon as an earlier adjustment clears the blocker.
Keeping the Prompt Cache Warm Prompt caching works by matching exact prefixes from the start of a request. Keeping system instructions and earlier turns untouched while appending new messages at the end lets subsequent turns read the shared history at 5% of fresh-input pricing. Writing to the cache for the first time costs more upfront: 1.25× fresh-input price for a 5-minute cache and 2× for a 1-hour cache. Reading a 120K cached context costs roughly $0.02, whereas writing that same 120K context into a 5-minute cache costs about $0.60.
Cache lifetime is 1 hour on subscription plans (dropping to 5 minutes while burning extra usage credits) and 5 minutes by default on API keys. Pausing longer than that window expires the cache. Switching models mid-session, attaching an MCP tool server, or compacting the conversation via /compact also changes the prompt prefix and triggers a fresh cache write.
Running /compact summarizes a long conversation so future turns carry fewer input tokens. Compacting at 150K tokens while the cache is still warm costs roughly $0.25 and trims about $0.025 per subsequent turn, paying for itself within ten turns. Waiting until after a 5-minute cache expires pushes the input cost of /compact alone to around $0.75, so run it before stepping away rather than after returning.
Pick your model, effort, and tool servers before starting a task, then leave them alone while the session runs.
Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation, not part of the original post.
Watching the total bill is not enough; you need to see which bucket spent the tokens. Checking cache share in /usage tells you whether prefix reuse held up, comparing output volume against input flags heavy generation or thinking spend, and comparing cumulative input against current conversation size reveals how many turns the loop ran. If you build custom agents, logging those three ratios per run makes cost spikes much easier to diagnose.
Giving an agent deterministic verification tools cuts expensive retry turns before you ever touch model tiers. In a data agent, for instance, attaching a schema-aware SQL checker catches bad column names or join keys before query execution fails blindly. When an agent loops on errors, ask what self-check tool is missing before reaching for a pricier model.
Lock in shared instructions and active tool definitions at session start. Because prefix caching breaks whenever earlier content changes, appending new context and tool results to the tail of the prompt rather than rewriting system state mid-run keeps cache hit rates high.
What to Try First Run claude update and confirm your CLI is on v2.1.280 or newer. Give Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 the exact same real task, then compare output quality alongside turn count, output tokens, and total cost in /usage. Check your current setting with /effort status. Start clearly scoped tasks at medium and step up only when test failures show the model needs deeper reasoning. Run /mcp before starting a task to review connected tool servers and turn off any servers you do not need for that session. Original post: What a task costs on Opus 5.5
summary: How Opus 5.5’s API price cuts translate into real task costs, and how to manage effort levels, model choice, and prompt caching to finish the same work for less.
title: Cutting Claude Code Costs: Start with Turn Counts and Prompt Cache Hits

content:
Turning up effort in Claude Code makes runs noticeably longer — but does the output improve in proportion to the wait? effort tells the model how much compute budget to spend on a task. Before defaulting to the highest level, it helps to see whether those extra minutes go toward better implementation, deeper verification, or unrequested features. This digest examines Thariq Shihipar’s experiments running identical tasks across effort levels.
At a Glance Raising effort gives the model more room to test, compare approaches, and verify its own work — increasing both runtime and token spend. Gains were sharpest in edge-case-heavy work such as security, hardware, and bug hunting. Higher effort does not rescue misunderstood requirements; if the direction is wrong, the model spends longer building the wrong thing. The author’s workflow: have Claude ask clarifying questions first, build a quick draft at low, confirm direction, and switch to high for verification. About the Original Post Thariq Shihipar published this guide on the claude.dev blog on 2026-09-25. It combines side-by-side Opus 5.5 runs across effort settings with Terminal-Bench 3.0 benchmark results for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5. It is written for Claude Code users who want concrete criteria for switching /effort rather than leaving it on a single setting.
Effort Signals How Much Budget to Spend Think of effort as a compute and verification budget rather than an intelligence dial.
The author compares it to a deadline. Given 12 hours for an assignment, you weigh tradeoffs, test edge cases, and double-check every assumption; given 1 hour, you ship the core path first. effort works the same way: low does not instruct the model to be sloppy, while higher settings widen how much self-checking and exploration it performs before finishing.
You can switch among low, medium, high, and max mid-conversation with /effort. On current models, changing effort mid-session preserves the prompt cache, so switching levels in a long thread does not force you to pay full re-prefill costs on prior context.
What Changed on Everyday Prompts Running the same prompts on Opus 5.5 across low, medium, high, and max produced clear behavioral differences:
Underspecified prompt: Asked simply to build a workout logging app, Opus 5.5 ran for 1.5m (low), 4m (medium), 11m (high), and 67m (max). low built workout logging and basic charts; max added activity-intensity heatmaps and made far more unprompted product decisions along the way. Constrained UI redesign: Asked to redesign the /config menu, low (1m) produced a rough layout sketch to test the concept, whereas max (28m) built a polished mockup closely matching the real Claude Code interface. For quick directional feedback, the author preferred low. Tightly specified prompt: After Claude interviewed the user to lock down a detailed spec first, runtimes still spread across low (16m), medium (22m), high (33m), and max (79m) — but core design and implementation converged, differing mainly in polish and small details. When the prompt was vague, higher effort changed the shape of the product; once the spec was tight, higher effort mostly changed runtime and finish quality.
That observation drives the author’s two-step loop: let Claude interview you to surface missing requirements, implement the first pass at low, and inspect the result. If the direction misses, refine the spec without having burned an hour; once the direction looks right, raise /effort to high so Claude hunts down subtle bugs.
What Changed on Hard Benchmark Tasks On harder engineering benchmarks, extra verification turned outright failures into passes. In html-js-filter — stripping covert JavaScript payloads from HTML — Fable 5.1 passed 1 out of 5 runs at low and 5 out of 5 at xhigh (a benchmark level above high).
At low, the model wrote a filter in roughly 2 minutes, tested it against a single synthetic HTML page, and stopped. In one high run the author inspected, the model spent roughly 33 minutes probing its draft with adversarial payloads, reading the underlying HTML parser’s source code, running standard XSS test vectors, and writing a fuzzer to generate random malformed documents. low checked one happy path; high attacked its own draft from multiple angles.
Opus 5.5 showed a similar gap on several Terminal-Bench tasks:
Benchmark task Pass count at low Pass count at higher setting Verification skipped at low mvcc-lsm-compaction 0/5 xhigh 4/5 Edited code directly without building or reproducing the bug first cli-2ph-simplex 0/5 high 5/5 Tested only a handful of small inputs gsea-proteomics 0/5 high 4/5 Picked one data preprocessing method without comparing alternatives Across all three tasks, the decisive difference was edge-case verification: fuzzing, larger test inputs, and comparing preprocessing choices before committing.
Over the full Terminal-Bench 3.0 suite, Fable 5.1 ran 370 attempts per setting. Passed attempts rose from 140 at low to 214 at max, while median tokens per attempt climbed from 73k to 222k.
Failure breakdowns revealed an important tradeoff. Failures caused by missed edge cases fell from 59 to 24, whereas failures from misreading requirements and pursuing the wrong approach climbed from 25 to 47. Extra verification catches bugs inside a chosen approach, not a misread spec.
Domain pass rates — grouping the lowest two settings against the highest three — jumped from 34% to 75% in Hardware and from 64% to 87% in Security, while Operations rose only from 12% to 22%. Tasks governed by fixed runbooks or procedural rules gained far less from open-ended exploration. Because these runs used an internal evaluation harness, per-task pass counts may differ slightly from the public leaderboard.
Domain Pass rate (lower effort) Pass rate (higher effort) Security 64% 87% Hardware 34% 75% ML 54% 73% Science 41% 61% Software 43% 56% Media 18% 30% Operations 12% 22% Figure 1. Median tokens per attempt (log scale) on the x-axis versus pass rate on the y-axis across effort settings (low through max). Original geometry and data points are preserved with English labels. Source: Original post.
Note the log scale on the horizontal axis: equal visual steps represent multiplying token usage rather than adding a fixed amount. Moving right spends more tokens; moving up passes more attempts, with Hardware showing the widest jump across domains.
How the Author Picks Effort Levels Low: Fast interactive back-and-forth while you are watching the terminal — brainstorming, quick UI sketches, small edits. Medium: Everyday software engineering work such as implementing a well-scoped feature. High: Tasks with tricky edge cases or heavy verification demands, such as fixing bugs in an existing codebase. Max: Unattended runs on hard problems — building and verifying an entire app end-to-end or auditing core software for security vulnerabilities. Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation rather than claims from the original post.
Higher effort pays off most when the model has a concrete way to test and falsify its own draft. Although effort does not control verification exclusively, the benchmark wins came from fuzzing, adversarial inputs, and comparing candidate methods. In SQL generation or data pipeline work, turning effort up makes sense once Claude has test queries, row-count invariants, or schema checks it can actually run against the output.
Clarifying requirements beats cranking up compute on an ambiguous prompt. Misread-spec failures nearly doubled at max, whereas locking down a spec through a short Q&A pass made low and max converge on nearly the same architecture. Spend five minutes tightening the spec before spending an hour of max tokens.
Match effort to whether a human is in the loop. As the original post notes on the proteomics task, an interactive user could have answered which preprocessing method to use in seconds instead of making the model test multiple pipelines on its own. Use low when you are sitting at the keyboard steering decisions, and reserve high or max for autonomous runs where Claude has to resolve edge cases without you.
What to Try First On your next feature task, ask Claude to interview you about missing requirements before writing code. Implement the first pass at low, confirm the architecture matches what you wanted, and then switch /effort to high for edge-case verification and testing. Take one stubborn bug and run the exact same prompt at medium and high in separate worktrees. Compare how each run reproduces the failure and what tests it writes before declaring the fix done. Review the logs from a recent failed unattended run and classify whether it missed an edge case or misunderstood the spec. Feed missed edge cases into your test suite, and fix spec misunderstandings in the prompt rather than raising effort. Original post: Using Claude Code: Spending your effort
summary: What Claude Code’s effort setting actually changes under the hood, where low and max diverge, and how Thariq Shihipar’s experiments map effort levels to real engineering work.
title: Effort Is Verification Time, Not Intelligence: Choosing Claude Code Effort Levels

content:
Asking Claude to “make the app faster” rarely works if you cannot name which user action is slow or what target number counts as a win. Anthropic’s team started by instrumenting how long it took to open the app and send a message. Once they had repeatable numbers, Claude could edit code, check whether latency dropped, and iterate. This digest walks through how they measured performance and shipped thousands of changes safely.
At a Glance During a focused two-week sprint in August 2026, Anthropic sped up core user actions across claude.ai and the Claude desktop app by roughly 3x. Clear before-and-after metrics let Claude run tight edit-and-verify loops on its own. The team merged more than 3,000 changes with zero customer-facing incidents or rollbacks. Humans focused on setting ambition levels, judging UI feel, and keeping parallel workstreams from colliding. About the Original Post Authors: Raymond Wang, Sam Attard, Issac G. / Published: 2026-09-23 Source: How we made claude.ai 3x faster in two weeksBest for: Developers figuring out how to bound and verify AI-authored code changes, and engineers working on frontend latency. What Got Faster, and by How Much The team targeted four user journeys that account for 95% of activity: launching the app, starting a new conversation, loading an existing conversation, and sending a message.
Across web, desktop, and product surfaces, they tracked 13 distinct checkpoints. Speedups averaged 3.1x (geometric mean across all 13 measurements), though individual gains varied widely. Selected p75 latencies — the time within which 3 out of 4 runs finish — moved as shown below:
claude.ai web initial load, time to interactive input: 3,085 ms to 550 ms Desktop app cold start: 6,310 ms to 3,328 ms Loading a Claude Cowork cloud session: 2,566 ms to 728 ms Figure 1. Latency improvements across 4 user journeys and 13 checkpoints, preserving the original chart’s geometry and p75 figures. Bar lengths show before-and-after latency alongside speedup multipliers and percentage reductions. Source: Original post.
The largest percentage drop came from sending a message in Claude Cowork on desktop (cloud), which fell from 928 ms to 48 ms (95%). The smallest was starting a conversation in web Chat, moving from 416 ms to 273 ms (34%).
The entire sprint ran out of a single Slack channel wired to Claude Tag (beta) backed by an internal research model roughly comparable to Opus 5.5. Claude hunted bottlenecks, wrote reproducible benchmarks, proposed fixes, and checked post-deploy telemetry. Roughly twenty projects were scoped at kickoff, and 12 of the 13 targets were hit by day four.
One standout change pre-rendered the message composer in plain HTML so users could start typing immediately instead of waiting for React hydration to wire up event handlers. Another cut sidebar re-renders by 90%.
Measuring Speed in the Lab Real-user telemetry only arrives after deployment, which is far too slow for an inner optimization loop. The team needed a local signal Claude could run in seconds. Wall-clock timing fluctuates with background machine load, so they measured CPU instruction counts for deterministic runs and paired them with wall-clock checks to confirm user-visible impact.
Instruction drops still had to prove they reduced real wait time. In one case, code assembling the conversation message tree looked up the same message ID three times; collapsing that to a single lookup cut instructions by 48% and wall-clock time by 78%.
Validated benchmarks went straight into CI with ratchets — upper-bound thresholds that tighten automatically as numbers improve and block any PR that regresses past the new ceiling. Benchmarks that proved flaky across runs or failed to track real latency were discarded. In Claude Code’s status-line scanner, for example, a fix reduced instructions by 31% and wall-clock time by 44%, after which a daily job lowered the CI ceiling so subsequent commits could not give back the gain.
Work settled into a repeatable loop. Someone posted a slow trace or interaction in a Slack thread; Claude reproduced it in a benchmark and opened small, reviewable PRs. User-facing changes shipped behind feature flags. If post-deploy field telemetry improved, the CI ratchet tightened; if numbers regressed, the team flipped the flag off and tried another angle without a code rollback.
More than 150 Slack threads ran in parallel and surfaced some surprising culprits. In the message composer, every keystroke was tangled up with 6,900 React hooks and 900 store subscriptions. Elsewhere, a buried location.reload() call was triggering 500,000 full page reloads every day.
Syntax highlighting hid another bottleneck. Whenever a response contained non-Latin-1 characters such as an em dash, V8 promoted the entire string to two-byte UTF-16 storage, slowing down regex scans during highlighting. A 20-line change that copied code blocks into one-byte strings before highlighting cut main-thread blocking on the first code block from 1.0s to 0.35s in lab tests — removing a noticeable UI freeze during streaming.
Figure 2. Before (left) and after (right) on a 4G-throttled connection: time to interactive input dropped from 2.93s to 0.36s. A lightweight HTML input appears immediately and hands off typed text once the full React composer hydrates. Source: Original post.
Guardrails and Human Roles Every PR required automated review plus human approval, and unit tests were written before optimization code touched existing logic. User-visible changes went out behind short-lived feature flags, while higher-risk changes rolled out in stages: internal employees first, then 1% of users, then 100%. Nearly 200 flags accumulated during the sprint, and Claude cleaned up more than half of them before the two weeks ended.
Humans concentrated on three things:
Setting ambition: Claude defaults to conservative, localized edits. Raymond pushed it toward bolder refactors by promising to merge and deploy immediately if the PR passed checks. Judging product feel: Designated thread owners made UX calls that benchmarks cannot capture, such as whether streaming tables cell by cell felt smooth or distracting. Coordinating parallel work: Engineers kept threads narrowly scoped, merged overlapping investigations, and shut down threads that hit diminishing returns. Streaming rendering on 120Hz displays — where each frame gets an 8.33ms budget — showed how human judgment and agent iteration reinforced each other. Across nearly 60 PRs in a single thread, the team measured frame times on long responses and drove main-thread blocking down from roughly 750ms to roughly 200ms.
Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation rather than claims from the original post.
Delegating optimization to an agent starts with a metric the agent can run and verify itself. “Make the app faster” gives Claude no stopping rule; “lower p75 time-to-interactive on initial load” gives it a clear scoreboard. The same principle applies to data pipelines and backend services: once before-and-after behavior is measurable under fixed conditions, an agent can iterate without human guesswork on every turn.
Proxy metrics in dev need a reality check against user-perceived latency. Counting CPU instructions, database calls, or React re-renders gives fast, low-noise feedback in CI, but optimizing a proxy in isolation can leave real wait times untouched. Pair deterministic CI ratchets with field telemetry so production numbers make the final call.
High-throughput agent shipping depends on cheap reversal paths. Feature flags, staged rollouts, and ratcheted CI thresholds let Anthropic merge over 3,000 changes in two weeks without a rollback. Build the kill switch and regression gate before turning an agent loose on a wide surface area.
Clear targets, field validation, and fast reversal mechanisms work as a package — skip one, and an agent can easily spend days shaving down the wrong number.
What to Try First Pick one noticeably slow interaction in your service and define exact start and end markers, such as button click to interactive input. Script a repeatable local measurement for that path — capturing both wall-clock time and a deterministic count like queries, API calls, or component renders — so code edits can be compared apples-to-apples. Gate agent-authored performance changes behind a feature flag and verify you can revert to the prior code path cleanly by toggling config alone. Original post: How we made claude.ai 3x faster in two weeks
summary: How Anthropic used a single Slack channel and Claude to make claude.ai and its desktop app roughly 3x faster in two weeks — what they measured, what guardrails held, and where humans stayed in the loop.

When Claude stops mid-task just to announce its next step, you end up nudging it forward turn by turn. Letting it run uninterrupted raises the opposite concern: how far will it go before you check the diff? This digest breaks down how to give Opus 5.5 explicit completion criteria and stop conditions, and why older prompt habits like “think step by step” are ready to retire.
At a Glance Hand over the full task in one request, state what counts as done, and specify when Claude should stop and ask. Drop phrases like “think carefully” from prompts and saved instructions. Opus 5.5 reasons on its own before every response. On long tasks, put continuation and stop rules in CLAUDE.md, fan out parallel checks to subagents, and keep a task checklist on disk. When a run finishes, read the items awaiting your input first, and watch for safety flags that can route a session to an older model. About the Original Post Addy Osmani published this Playbooks guide on the claude.dev blog on 2026-09-22. It is aimed at developers who already use the Claude app or Claude Code and want a concise breakdown of what changes with Opus 5.5.
1. Framing the Request The original post recommends sending the entire task together with its completion criteria. Its example is migrating payment API endpoints to a new client — stating upfront whether the job ends at updating endpoint URLs or includes deleting legacy client code and passing the test suite.
In that example, “done” means three things: every endpoint migrated, the old client removed, and the test suite green. The prompt also adds a stop condition: pause and ask if a test fails for an unexplained reason. That stop condition belongs to this specific migration example rather than serving as a blanket rule for every prompt.
According to the post, Opus 5.5 sustains multi-step work much longer than Opus 5. Early testers reported running multi-hour coding jobs largely hands-off.
Figure 1. From left to right: the delegated task, the completion criteria, and the stop condition. The job is only done once every payment endpoint is migrated, the legacy client is removed, and tests pass. Source: Original post.
The next recommendation is removing instructions like “think carefully” or “think step by step” from prompts and saved guidelines. Opus 5.5 reasons before answering and calibrates how much thinking a request needs on its own. In the author’s chat tests, cutting those phrases started responses faster without a noticeable drop in quality. When a task in Claude Code warrants deeper verification, adjust the effort setting instead.
If you think of an extra instruction mid-run in Claude Code, type it and press Enter — Claude picks it up while working.
Design prompts still fall back to a handful of default styles unless you give concrete direction. Asking Claude to “avoid generic styles” usually swaps one cliché layout for another. Name the exact patterns you want to skip, such as cream backgrounds, italic accent words in headings, or 01 / 02 / 03 section labels.
2. Managing Long Tasks in Claude Code During long sessions, Claude still occasionally announces its next step and stops, or asks whether to continue. To curb that habit, put explicit continuation rules in CLAUDE.md.
The post suggests two rules. First, keep moving through steps that do not need human input, and include the next action whenever reporting progress. Second, stop when human judgment is genuinely required or right before high-risk actions such as deleting data, force-pushing, or changing state outside the repository. Keep permission prompts enabled for destructive commands even when CLAUDE.md instructs Claude to continue automatically.
Larger audits split cleanly across subagents. When checking several services for the same bug pattern, assign one subagent per service and require each report to include both a verdict and supporting evidence. After verifying the cited code, compile the service name, status, and evidence into a single table so unchecked services stand out from verified ones.
Figure 2. Assign one subagent per service, verify the evidence in each report, and consolidate service, status, and evidence into a single table. Source: Original post.
Have Claude maintain its checklist in a file such as TASKS.md. When a long session fills the context window, Claude Code compacts older turns into a summary. Writing completed and remaining items to disk keeps progress intact across compaction and gives you a direct file to inspect.
3. Reviewing the Output When Opus 5.5 finishes a long run, scan first for items waiting on your call — open design decisions or changes that need explicit sign-off. Compared with Opus 5, Opus 5.5 separates what it changed, what it found, and where it needs human input much more clearly.
Running an AI code review before your own pass also pays off. One early tester reported that Opus 5.5 at its lowest effort level caught more bugs and produced fewer false positives than Opus 5 at high effort. Treat that comparison as one tester’s observation rather than a published benchmark.
When asking for a review, scope it to issues that must be fixed before merge, and require the file, line number, failure reason, and reproduction steps for each item. For research or debugging tasks, ask Claude to list both where it checked and what it could not verify. Knowing a path was inspected and came up empty still narrows your search.
In the Claude app, confirm that Opus 5.5 is active in the model selector first. Attach charts and screenshots directly as images rather than retyping numbers; Opus 5.5 reads spatial layout — such as which boxes an arrow connects — more accurately than Opus 5. Cross-checking long documents for internal contradictions is another strong fit: in the author’s tests, Opus 5.5 spotted a date paired with the wrong day of the week inside a long planning thread and a slide chart whose bars did not match its labels. When you need a table or document, ask for the finished file instead of an outline.
4. Safety Flags and Fast Mode Opus 5.5 is the first Opus release shipped with Fable-level biological and cyber safety classifiers. When those classifiers flag a message for inspection, most sessions automatically switch to an older model to continue the task. Anthropic notes that benign work can still trigger false positives and that threshold tuning is ongoing.
In the Claude app, you can reselect Opus 5.5 in the model picker, though starting a new conversation works better because an earlier flagged message in history can trip the filter again. If you want Claude to ask before switching models, turn off model fallback under Capabilities in Settings. In Claude Code, run /model to switch back, press Esc twice to edit and resend your last prompt, adjust fallback behavior in /config, and report false positives via /feedback. Avoid asking the model to copy its internal reasoning verbatim into the final reply — that request can be refused and falls into a flagged category.
For interactive work with frequent back-and-forth turns, Claude Code includes fast mode (/fast), which runs the same model at higher output speed. At publication time, fast mode was in research preview, required extra usage enabled, and carried a higher per-token rate than standard mode, so weigh latency gains against token cost.
Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation rather than claims from the original post.
Pairing every delegated task with verifiable completion criteria cuts down turn-by-turn micromanagement. In data pipeline work, for instance, stating the expected output schema and the exact test suite to pass lets Claude check its own work before handing control back.
Autonomous runs still need pre-agreed checkpoints. Decide upfront when Claude should pause to ask, which commands always require human confirmation, and where progress lives on disk. When delegating across subagents, verify the cited lines rather than trusting summary verdicts alone. That structure separates routine execution from decisions that genuinely need a human.
Most performance comparisons in the original post come from early-adopter anecdotes and lightweight author tests. Even the claim that low-effort Opus 5.5 beat high-effort Opus 5 on bug finding lacks published test conditions. Run a few representative tasks from your own codebase across both models before rewriting team defaults.
What to Try First Audit your saved prompts and CLAUDE.md files for phrases like “think carefully” or “think step by step.” Send the same task to Opus 5.5 with and without those lines to compare time-to-first-token and output quality on your own workload. Add explicit continuation and pause rules to CLAUDE.md — for example: “Continue through steps that do not require my input, but stop and ask when a decision is ambiguous or before deleting data, force-pushing, or modifying anything outside this repository.” On your next multi-step task, include concrete completion criteria, ask Claude to log completed and remaining items in TASKS.md, and start your review with the section listing items that need your input. Original post: Getting the most out of Opus 5.5 in Claude and Claude Code
summary: Opus 5.5 works longer on its own and decides how much to reason before answering. Here is how to update your prompting habits, structure long Claude Code runs, and review what comes back.
title: Delegating Work to Opus 5.5: Start with Clear Completion Criteria
